Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, it appears that Stage I non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) is indeed considered a relatively early-stage cancer. Several studies suggest that patients with tumors measuring 3 cm or less in size and adenocarcinoma histologic type have a more favorable prognosis compared to those with larger tumors.

In fact, one study found that even with adenocarcinoma, the 5-year survival rate for Stage I NSCLC is still relatively high. Furthermore, other studies indicate that negative bronchial resection margins and smaller tumor size are associated with better outcomes.

However, it's essential to note that the prognosis of early-stage NSCLC can vary depending on several factors, such as performance status, weight loss, and overall health. Additionally, while some studies have shown a positive correlation between tumor size and survival rates, others have found no association.

Overall, based on these healthcare Q&A matches, it seems that Stage I non-small cell lung carcinoma is indeed considered an early-stage cancer, with significant advances in diagnosis and treatment being available to improve patient outcomes.
